Synthetic research report for functional demonstrations; measurements are invented.

# Chapter 1: Marsh drainage study

This report investigates whether opening blocked tidal channels changes the duration
of standing water in a coastal restoration site. It distinguishes hydrological
measurements from claims about habitat recovery.

## Methods

The team installed water-level loggers in six paired plots. One plot in each pair
received a reopened drainage channel; the other retained the blocked channel.
Loggers sampled every fifteen minutes during eight weeks of the spring season.
Two sensors failed during a storm. Their missing intervals were excluded rather
than filled with predicted values. The study did not sample a full annual cycle.

## Results

Median standing-water duration was eighteen hours per tidal cycle in the blocked
plots and eleven hours in the reopened plots. The comparison uses the four pairs
with complete records. It is an association observed during the measurement period;
the study did not establish that drainage caused an improvement in bird nesting.

## Conclusion

Reopening channels was associated with shorter standing-water duration during
spring. The missing storm records and absence of winter measurements limit the
conclusion. The authors recommend a full year of monitoring before expansion.

# Chapter 2: Salinity and vegetation

This chapter considers a different response to tidal restoration: salt exposure.

## Methods

Field staff collected weekly pore-water samples at fixed distances from each
channel. Vegetation observations recorded cover, not plant survival or growth.

## Results

Median salinity increased from twelve to nineteen parts per thousand near reopened
channels. Salt-sensitive plants showed less cover there, while salt-tolerant cover
was stable. The short observation period cannot separate seasonal changes from
effects of channel reopening.

## Conclusion

Reduced standing water should not be treated as universal ecological improvement.
Hydrology and vegetation can respond differently. A later review should compare
both chapters before recommending further channel work.
